title: Harmony and Voice Leading I: Chord Function, Cadence, and Phrase

guide.summary: Unit 4 introduces harmonic function, cadences, phrases and periods, and the rules of four-part (SATB) voice leading in common-practice style.

sections.heading: Function and cadences
sections.body: Chords group into functions: tonic (I, vi), predominant (IV, ii), and dominant (V, vii°). The basic phrase model moves T → PD → D → T. Cadences end phrases: perfect authentic (PAC: V–I, both root position, soprano ending on 1), imperfect authentic (IAC: V–I with soprano on 3 or 5, or an inverted chord), half cadence (HC: ends on V), plagal (IV–I), and deceptive (V–vi). A cadential 6/4 (I6/4 resolving to V) decorates the dominant; it functions as part of V.

sections.heading: Phrases and periods
sections.body: A phrase is a musical thought ending with a cadence. A period pairs an antecedent phrase (usually ending with a weaker cadence such as HC) with a consequent ending more strongly (PAC). A parallel period's phrases begin alike; a contrasting period's do not. Phrases can be extended by repetition or a deceptive cadence.

sections.heading: Voice leading
sections.body: Ranges: soprano C4–G5, alto G3–D5, tenor C3–G4, bass E2–C4. Keep no more than an octave between soprano–alto and alto–tenor. Avoid parallel (consecutive) perfect fifths and octaves between any two voices, and direct fifths/octaves in outer voices unless the soprano moves by step. Avoid voice crossing and overlap. In root-position triads, double the root; never double the leading tone. Resolve the leading tone up to tonic when in an outer voice and chordal sevenths down by step. Prefer common tones and stepwise motion in upper voices; contrary motion between bass and soprano is strongest.

sections.heading: Worked example: checking for parallels
sections.body: After writing four voices, check every pair (S–A, S–T, S–B, A–T, A–B, T–B) between consecutive chords. Parallel fifths occur when two voices a perfect fifth apart move to another perfect fifth in the same direction, such as bass C to D and tenor G to A. Fix them by changing one voice's motion, often by moving upper voices in contrary motion to the bass or keeping a common tone. Parallel octaves are fixed the same way. Also check outer voices for direct (hidden) fifths and octaves when the soprano leaps.

sections.heading: Harmonic dictation strategies
sections.body: In harmonic dictation, you will hear a progression and write the bass and soprano lines and Roman numerals. Listen first for the bass line, which reveals chord roots and inversions, then the soprano. Recognize common patterns: I–IV–V–I, I–ii6–V–I, I–vi–IV–V, cadential 6/4 to V, and deceptive V–vi. Use the cadences as anchors, since phrases usually end on I or V.

sections.heading: Phrase and cadence on the exam
sections.body: Aural questions often ask you to identify cadence types. A PAC sounds final, with the melody ending on the tonic; an IAC sounds less final; a half cadence sounds like a pause on V; a deceptive cadence surprises by moving to vi; a plagal cadence (IV–I) has an 'amen' quality.

sections.heading: Common errors
sections.body: Students double the leading tone, space upper voices more than an octave apart, and forget to resolve tendency tones.

sections.heading: Worked example: a complete progression
sections.body: Realizing I–IV–V–I in C major, a good voicing is soprano C5–C5–B4–C5, alto G4–A4–G4–G4, tenor E4–F4–D4–E4, and bass C3–F3–G3–C3. The soprano holds a common tone from I to IV, the upper voices move down against the rising bass from IV to V, and the leading tone resolves up in the final chord. Every chord doubles its root, and there are no parallel fifths or octaves.

sections.heading: Sight-singing connection
sections.body: Singing cadences helps you hear them. Practice singing the bass line of common progressions and arpeggiating chords; this trains your ear for harmonic dictation and cadence identification.

sections.heading: Key terms
sections.body: Know tonic, predominant, dominant, PAC, IAC, half cadence, plagal cadence, deceptive cadence, cadential 6/4, phrase, period, parallel fifths and octaves, and voice crossing.

sections.heading: Practice routine
sections.body: Write one short four-part progression each day and check every pair of voices for parallels. Listen to chorales by Bach and identify the cadence at the end of each phrase, noting whether it is authentic, half, plagal, or deceptive.

sections.heading: Free-response connection
sections.body: Part writing from Roman numerals tests exactly these rules.

keyTakeaways: Double the root; don't double the leading tone.
commonMistakes: Calling any V–I a PAC (check inversions and soprano).
Spacing over an octave between upper voices.
Doubling the leading tone in V.
examTips: Check every pair of voices for parallels.
Identify the soprano's last note for cadence type.
Use common tones to keep voices smooth.

practice.prompt: In C major, realize the progression I – IV – V – I in four voices (SATB), all chords in root position. Give each voice's pitch, avoid parallel fifths and octaves, and name the cadence.

rubric.description: I: e.g., S C5, A G4, T E4, B C3.
IV: e.g., S C5, A A4, T F4, B F3.
V: e.g., S B4, A G4, T D4, B G3 (leading tone not doubled).
I: e.g., S C5, A G4, T E4, B C3.
I→IV smooth, common tone C held, no parallels.
IV→V upper voices move contrary to the bass, no parallels.
V→I leading tone B up to C, no parallels.
PAC: V–I root position, soprano ends on tonic.

practice.sampleResponse:
Chord 1 (I): S C5, A G4, T E4, B C3.
Chord 2 (IV): S C5, A A4, T F4, B F3.
Chord 3 (V): S B4, A G4, T D4, B G3.
Chord 4 (I): S C5, A G4, T E4, B C3.
The soprano holds C over the I–IV connection, then the upper voices move down by step against the rising bass from IV to V (contrary motion avoids parallels). In V–I, the leading tone B rises to C in the soprano while the bass falls a fifth. Every chord doubles its root, and the leading tone is not doubled. The cadence is a perfect authentic cadence.
